description: issue #688 (terminal slice, review round 2): a word that PARSES as a number is accepted where `wait` expects a number, AND is used as that number. `spec/execution-model.md:33-34` makes this a normative CORE rule (`Words that parse as numbers are accepted where a number is expected`), and nothing in `spec/interaction-events.md`'s `### wait <n>` opts the profile out of it. The pause is measured with a bare-numeric `every 1` timer registered first: `wait "2"` must advance the tick clock by exactly 2, so the handler fires exactly TWICE (ticks 1 and 2) before the `wait` `primitive` event, then `print "done"` runs. Round 1 of this fixture asserted only that `wait "2"` was accepted and did not fault, which an implementation that accepted the word but paused for 0 or 1 ticks would have satisfied with a byte-identical stream (review round 2 finding); counting the timer's invocations is what turns acceptance into proof of the VALUE, matching how the `every` sibling proves its own coercion by firing on schedule. This is the POSITIVE complement of `wait-non-number-type-error`: without it the corpus recorded only that a word is rejected, so an implementation that rejected EVERY word -- violating the Core coercion rule -- would have passed the whole corpus while the negative looked like proof that words are simply illegal here. The two together draw the line where the spec draws it: parses-as-a-number is accepted and honored, does-not-parse is `ol-type`.
